title: Tingling in Hands: Causes, When to Worry and the Blood Tests That Check
summary: Tingling in hands or numb fingers? See when to call 911, what one hand versus both hands suggests, and how B12, HbA1c and thyroid tests find the cause.
body_markdown:
Table of contents


**Tingling or numbness in the hands most often comes from pressure on a nerve: a hand that “falls asleep” after you lean on it, or a nerve squeezed at the wrist or elbow, as in carpal tunnel syndrome** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003206.htm) \]\[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000433.htm) \]. This kind of tingling usually affects part of one hand and fades once the pressure is off.


**Tingling that keeps coming back in both hands, or in the hands and the feet, points to something affecting nerves throughout the body** \[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000593.htm) \]\[[4](https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/peripheral-neuropathy) \]. The common medical causes are a low vitamin B12 level, high blood sugar from diabetes, an underactive thyroid, kidney disease, abnormal calcium, too little or too much vitamin B6 and, more rarely, low copper \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003206.htm) \]\[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000593.htm) \]\[[4](https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/peripheral-neuropathy) \]. Blood tests check each of these: vitamin B12 with methylmalonic acid (MMA), HbA1c, TSH, a comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) for kidney function and calcium, vitamin B6 and copper \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003206.htm) \]\[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000574.htm) \]\[[6](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560728/) \].


## When tingling in hands is an emergency


**Call 911 right away for sudden numbness or weakness in the face, arm or leg, especially on one side of the body** \[[7](https://www.cdc.gov/stroke/signs-symptoms/index.html) \]. That is a sign of stroke. The other sudden signs of stroke are \[[7](https://www.cdc.gov/stroke/signs-symptoms/index.html) \]:


- confusion, trouble speaking, or trouble understanding speech;
- trouble seeing in one or both eyes;
- trouble walking, dizziness, loss of balance or lack of coordination;
- a severe headache with no known cause.


The CDC’s B.E. F.A.S.T. check helps: loss of **B** alance, **E** ye changes, a drooping **F** ace when the person smiles, one **A** rm that drifts down when both are raised, slurred **S** peech, and **T** ime to call 911 \[[7](https://www.cdc.gov/stroke/signs-symptoms/index.html) \]. Do not drive yourself or let someone drive you to the hospital. An ambulance team can start treatment on the way \[[7](https://www.cdc.gov/stroke/signs-symptoms/index.html) \].


**Also go to a hospital or call 911 if** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003206.htm) \]:


- the numbness or tingling comes with weakness or you are unable to move;
- it starts just after a head, neck or back injury;
- you cannot control the movement of an arm or a leg, or you lose bladder or bowel control;
- you are confused or have lost consciousness, even briefly.


None of these signs should wait for a blood test. The tests in this article are for tingling that comes and goes or builds slowly, never for sudden symptoms.


## Reading the pattern: one hand, both hands, or hands and feet


**Where the tingling is, and when it happens, narrows the cause before any test is ordered.** Doctors start with exactly these questions: when it began, where it is, and what makes it better or worse \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003206.htm) \].


Pattern Likely causes What checks it


Part of one hand, or worse at night or after leaning on it Pressure on one nerve: carpal tunnel syndrome at the wrist, the ulnar nerve at the elbow \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000433.htm) \]\[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000789.htm) \] A clinician’s exam of the hand and wrist, with nerve tests if needed. Diagnosed by exam, not a blood test \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000433.htm) \]


Both hands, or the hands and feet, building over weeks or months Low B12, high blood sugar, underactive thyroid, kidney disease, low calcium, B6, low copper \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003206.htm) \]\[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000593.htm) \]\[[4](https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/peripheral-neuropathy) \] Vitamin B12 with MMA, HbA1c, TSH, CMP for kidney function and calcium, vitamin B6, copper \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003206.htm) \]\[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000574.htm) \]\[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003565.htm) \]\[[6](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560728/) \]


Both hands, face or feet, during fast breathing or panic Hyperventilation from anxiety or a panic attack \[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003071.htm) \]\[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000924.htm) \] The pattern itself. Tingling settles when breathing slows \[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003071.htm) \]


Sudden, on one side of the body Stroke or TIA \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003206.htm) \]\[[7](https://www.cdc.gov/stroke/signs-symptoms/index.html) \] Call 911


Tingling in both hands at once is less likely to come from one squeezed nerve, although carpal tunnel syndrome can affect both hands \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000433.htm) \]. Tingling that starts in the toes and feet and later reaches the fingers is the typical path of nerve damage from diabetes \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000693.htm) \].


## Hands going numb while sleeping


**Numb hands at night are usually caused by the position you sleep in.** Staying in one position for a long time, or pressing on part of the body, can compress a nerve and cause numbness and tingling \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003206.htm) \]. For carpal tunnel symptoms, the first steps include not sleeping on your wrists and wearing a wrist splint at night \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000433.htm) \]. Leaning on an elbow for a long time presses on the ulnar nerve, and its pain or numbness can wake you from sleep \[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000789.htm) \].


A hand that “falls asleep” and recovers within minutes once you move is not a sign of disease \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003206.htm) \]. Numbness that wakes you most nights, or that is still there during the day, is worth getting examined. A clinician can tell which nerve is involved from which fingers go numb \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000433.htm) \]\[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000789.htm) \].


## Carpal tunnel syndrome and other pinched nerves


**Carpal tunnel syndrome is numbness, tingling or pain in the thumb, index finger, middle finger and the thumb side of the ring finger, caused by pressure on the median nerve at the wrist** \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000433.htm) \]. It can affect one or both hands. Other signs are a weak grip, clumsiness when gripping objects, trouble with fine finger movements and pain that spreads up toward the elbow \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000433.htm) \].


It is most common in people aged 30 to 60, and more common in women than men \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000433.htm) \]. Repeating the same hand and wrist motion, using vibrating tools, wrist fractures or arthritis, obesity, rheumatoid arthritis, alcohol use and fluid retained during pregnancy or menopause can all contribute \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000433.htm) \].


**The little finger is a different nerve.** Numbness or tingling in the little finger and part of the ring finger points to the ulnar nerve, which runs past the elbow at the “funny bone” \[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000789.htm) \]. Long-term pressure on the elbow and diabetes are among its causes \[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000789.htm) \]. Pressure on nerves in the neck, such as from a herniated disk, can also cause numbness along the arm and hand \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003206.htm) \].


**Carpal tunnel syndrome is diagnosed with an exam, not a blood test.** A clinician checks where the numbness is and tests grip strength, and may tap over the nerve or hold your wrist bent for 60 seconds to see if that brings on symptoms \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000433.htm) \]. Nerve tests such as electromyography and nerve conduction studies can confirm it \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000433.htm) \]. Blood tests matter only when carpal tunnel comes with signs of a body-wide cause, or when the tingling is in both hands and the feet.


## Low vitamin B12


**A low vitamin B12 level that lasts a long time can damage nerves, and numbness and tingling of the hands and feet is one of the main signs** \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000574.htm) \]. Others are loss of balance, trouble concentrating, irritability and, in severe cases, confusion or memory changes \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000574.htm) \]. B12 deficiency can also cause anemia, with fatigue, pale skin and shortness of breath, but many people have mild symptoms or none \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000574.htm) \]. The National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) names vitamin B12 deficiency as one of the two best-known vitamin causes of nerve damage \[[4](https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/peripheral-neuropathy) \].


The body needs both enough B12 in food and the ability to absorb it. Low B12 is more likely with \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000574.htm) \]:


- pernicious anemia, an autoimmune condition that blocks B12 absorption in the stomach;
- surgery that removes part of the stomach or small intestine, including some weight-loss surgeries;
- Crohn disease, celiac disease and other conditions that affect digestion;
- a strict vegetarian diet;
- long-term use of metformin or of antacids and other heartburn medicines;
- alcohol use, or recreational use of nitrous oxide (laughing gas).


**Timing matters.** Nerve damage from low B12 may be permanent if treatment does not start promptly after symptoms begin \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000574.htm) \]. Among the vitamin levels checked for numbness and tingling, MedlinePlus singles out vitamin B12 \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003206.htm) \].


**The blood tests for B12 are a serum vitamin B12 level and, alongside it, methylmalonic acid (MMA)** \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000574.htm) \]\[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003565.htm) \]. MMA is a substance the body makes when it breaks down proteins, and a higher than normal MMA level may be due to B12 deficiency, which is why it is checked alongside the B12 level \[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003565.htm) \]. Low B12 is also the most common cause of subacute combined degeneration, a form of spinal cord damage that causes tingling, loss of sensation, weakness and trouble walking \[[6](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560728/) \]. For how doctors combine these results, see[how B12 deficiency is diagnosed](https://mitohealth.com/guide/b12-deficiency-diagnosis) , and for the background on the vitamin,[why vitamin B12 matters after 30](https://mitohealth.com/blog/vitamin-b12-essential-health-energy-after-30) .


## High blood sugar and diabetes


**Diabetes is the leading cause of peripheral neuropathy in the US** \[[4](https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/peripheral-neuropathy) \]. High blood sugar over a long time damages nerves, both directly and by reducing their blood flow \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000693.htm) \]. About one half of people with diabetes develop nerve damage \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000693.htm) \].


The symptoms usually start in the toes and feet as tingling, burning or deep pain, and over time can reach the fingers and hands \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000693.htm) \]. They often develop slowly, over years \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000693.htm) \]. Some people whose diabetes develops slowly already have nerve damage when they are first diagnosed \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000693.htm) \]. Diabetes is also one of the causes of ulnar nerve damage at the elbow \[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000789.htm) \].


**[HbA1c](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/hba1c) is the blood test that shows your average blood sugar over about the last 3 months** \[[13](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/hemoglobin-a1c-hba1c-test/) \]:


- below 5.7% is normal;
- 5.7% to 6.4% is prediabetes;
- 6.5% or higher is diabetes.


A doctor usually confirms diabetes with more than one test \[[13](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/hemoglobin-a1c-hba1c-test/) \]. A[fasting glucose](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/glucose) reading, which is part of the CMP, adds a single-moment view \[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/comprehensive-metabolic-panel-cmp/) \]. If you have tingling in both feet, or in the hands and feet, HbA1c is one of the first tests worth having. Mito offers an[HbA1c blood test](https://mitohealth.com/products/hemoglobin-a1c-with-reflex-to-1-5-anhydroglucitol-1-5-ag) .


## Underactive thyroid


**An underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism) is a listed cause of numbness and tingling** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003206.htm) \]\[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000593.htm) \]. NINDS explains that hormone imbalances can cause tissues to swell and press on the peripheral nerves \[[4](https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/peripheral-neuropathy) \].


Hypothyroidism usually comes with other changes that develop slowly: feeling cold when others do not, fatigue or feeling slowed down, constipation, dry skin, joint or muscle pain, and heavier or irregular periods \[[15](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000353.htm) \]. Because it develops slowly, many people do not notice the symptoms for months or years \[[16](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/tsh-thyroid-stimulating-hormone-test/) \].


**A TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) blood test checks how well your thyroid is working** \[[16](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/tsh-thyroid-stimulating-hormone-test/) \]. It shows whether the thyroid is making too little or too much hormone, but not why \[[16](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/tsh-thyroid-stimulating-hormone-test/) \]. Mito offers a[TSH blood test](https://mitohealth.com/products/thyroid-stimulating-hormone-tsh) . For which thyroid tests to add after TSH, see[the best thyroid test for you](https://mitohealth.com/guide/best-thyroid-test) .


## Kidney function and calcium


**Chronic kidney disease (CKD) can cause numbness in the hands and feet, usually once kidney function has dropped a lot** \[[17](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000471.htm) \]. When the kidneys fail to clear waste, toxins build up in the blood and can damage nerve tissue \[[4](https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/peripheral-neuropathy) \]. Most people on dialysis develop some form of peripheral neuropathy \[[4](https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/peripheral-neuropathy) \]. Early CKD often causes no symptoms at all, so it is usually found on blood and urine tests \[[17](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000471.htm) \].


**A low blood calcium level can cause tingling in the lips, tongue, fingers and feet, along with muscle cramps or spasms** \[[18](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/calcium-blood-test/) \]. Calcium is needed for nerves and muscles to work \[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/comprehensive-metabolic-panel-cmp/) \]. Low calcium has several causes, including problems with the parathyroid glands, low vitamin D, chronic kidney disease and low magnesium \[[19](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430912/) \]. When the parathyroid glands make too little hormone, tingling lips, fingers and toes are the most common symptom \[[20](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000385.htm) \]. Many people with an abnormal calcium level have no symptoms, so it is often found on a routine test \[[18](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/calcium-blood-test/) \]. Abnormal potassium and sodium levels are also listed causes of numbness and tingling \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003206.htm) \].


**One blood draw covers both.** The[Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)](https://mitohealth.com/products/comprehensive-metabolic-panel-cmp) measures[creatinine](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/creatinine) and urea nitrogen for kidney function, plus calcium, sodium, potassium and glucose \[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/comprehensive-metabolic-panel-cmp/) \]. Labs use creatinine to estimate your[eGFR](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/egfrcr) , the main number for kidney function \[[17](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000471.htm) \]. Because much of the calcium in blood is bound to albumin, a low total calcium is read alongside albumin, which the CMP also measures, and may be followed by an ionized calcium test \[[19](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430912/) \]\[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/comprehensive-metabolic-panel-cmp/) \].


## Vitamin B6: too little or too much


**Vitamin B6 is the vitamin where both a shortage and an excess can cause tingling** \[[21](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002402.htm) \]\[[4](https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/peripheral-neuropathy) \]. It helps maintain normal nerve function \[[21](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002402.htm) \].


- **Too little.** B6 deficiency can cause peripheral neuropathy, along with confusion, depression, irritability and a sore mouth and tongue \[[21](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002402.htm) \]. It is uncommon in the US \[[21](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002402.htm) \]. It is more likely with kidney failure, liver disease or heavy alcohol use \[[21](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002402.htm) \].
- **Too much.** Large doses of vitamin B6 can cause numbness, sensory changes and trouble coordinating movement \[[21](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002402.htm) \]. NINDS names excess vitamin B6, alongside low B12, as one of the best-known vitamin causes of nerve damage \[[4](https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/peripheral-neuropathy) \]. Food does not cause B6 toxicity: the reported cases come from high-dose supplements \[[22](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK554500/) \].


**The excess is easy to miss because B6 is in many products** , including multivitamins, and is added to some processed foods and nutritional powders \[[23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470579/) \]. If your hands or feet tingle and you take supplements, check their labels for vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) and bring the list to your doctor before stopping anything. A[vitamin B6 blood test](https://mitohealth.com/products/vitamin-b6) shows whether your level is low or high.


## Low copper


**Copper deficiency is a rare cause of nerve and spinal cord damage that looks a lot like B12 deficiency** \[[6](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560728/) \]. Copper helps keep nerves healthy and works with iron to form red blood cells, so a lack of copper can also cause anemia \[[24](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002419.htm) \]. Most people get enough copper from food \[[24](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002419.htm) \].


When copper deficiency damages the spinal cord, it causes the same picture as low B12: tingling, loss of sensation, weakness and trouble walking \[[6](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560728/) \]. One recognized cause is taking in too much zinc, which can lead to copper deficiency \[[6](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560728/) \]. StatPearls advises that unexplained anemia with nerve symptoms should prompt testing for B12 and, less commonly, copper in people at risk \[[6](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560728/) \].


**Copper is a reasonable next check when B12 is normal but symptoms point to nerve damage** , especially with high zinc intake or anemia. Mito offers a[copper blood test](https://mitohealth.com/products/copper) .


## Anxiety, panic and fast breathing


**Anxiety can cause real tingling in the hands, usually through fast, deep breathing (hyperventilation)** \[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003071.htm) \]. Overbreathing lowers the carbon dioxide level in the blood, which causes numbness and tingling in the arms or around the mouth, and muscle spasms in the hands and feet \[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003071.htm) \]. Losing carbon dioxide makes the blood more alkaline, and alkaline blood lowers the active, ionized form of calcium, which can cause tingling \[[25](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK545269/) \]. Numbness or tingling in the hands, feet or face is one of the listed symptoms of a panic attack \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000924.htm) \].


This tingling comes on with the anxious episode and settles as breathing slows \[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003071.htm) \]. It does not need a blood test to explain it. Rapid breathing for the first time may be a medical emergency and needs an emergency room right away \[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003071.htm) \]. Tingling that keeps happening outside anxious moments needs the checks above. For how anxiety and low mood overlap with blood results, see[anxiety and low mood: what your blood might be telling you](https://mitohealth.com/blog/anxiety-and-low-mood-what-your-blood-might-be-telling-you) .


## Which blood tests check the cause of tingling hands


**MedlinePlus lists the blood tests a provider may order for numbness and tingling: a complete blood count, glucose tests for diabetes, electrolytes and liver tests, thyroid tests, vitamin levels (particularly vitamin B12), heavy metal screening and markers of inflammation** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003206.htm) \]. Each likely cause maps to specific results:


Result What it suggests


Low vitamin B12, or a high MMA B12 deficiency is likely behind the tingling \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000574.htm) \]\[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003565.htm) \]


HbA1c of 6.5% or higher Diabetes, the leading cause of neuropathy \[[13](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/hemoglobin-a1c-hba1c-test/) \]\[[4](https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/peripheral-neuropathy) \]


HbA1c of 5.7% to 6.4% Prediabetes \[[13](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/hemoglobin-a1c-hba1c-test/) \]


High TSH An underactive thyroid \[[16](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/tsh-thyroid-stimulating-hormone-test/) \]


High creatinine with a low eGFR Reduced kidney function \[[17](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000471.htm) \]


Low calcium A calcium cause such as the parathyroid glands, low vitamin D, kidney disease or low magnesium \[[19](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430912/) \]


High vitamin B6 Excess B6, usually from supplements \[[21](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002402.htm) \]\[[22](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK554500/) \]


Low vitamin B6 B6 deficiency, often with kidney, liver or alcohol problems \[[21](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002402.htm) \]


Low copper, with B12 normal Copper deficiency, often from excess zinc \[[6](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560728/) \]


All normal The common blood causes are less likely; a nerve exam and nerve tests come next \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003206.htm) \]

## Is tingling in hands a sign of high blood pressure?


**High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms, so tingling hands are not a reliable sign of it** \[[26](https://medlineplus.gov/highbloodpressure.html) \]. Blood pressure is found by measuring it \[[26](https://medlineplus.gov/highbloodpressure.html) \]. High blood pressure is linked to tingling in two indirect ways. Narrowed arteries from high blood pressure or atherosclerosis can reduce blood flow to nerves and lead to neuropathy, and some medicines for heart disease and blood pressure occasionally cause neuropathy as a side effect \[[4](https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/peripheral-neuropathy) \]. High blood pressure also raises stroke risk, and sudden one-sided numbness is a stroke sign that needs 911 \[[7](https://www.cdc.gov/stroke/signs-symptoms/index.html) \].


## What diseases start with tingling in the hands?


**Several conditions can first show up as numbness or tingling in the hands** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003206.htm) \]\[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000593.htm) \]\[[4](https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/peripheral-neuropathy) \]:


- carpal tunnel syndrome;
- diabetes and prediabetes;
- vitamin B12 deficiency;
- an underactive thyroid;
- chronic kidney disease;
- multiple sclerosis, which affects the brain and spinal cord;
- autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or lupus;
- Raynaud phenomenon, in which the blood vessels in the fingers narrow in the cold;
- migraine, seizures, and stroke or TIA, which cause sudden rather than gradual symptoms.


Most of these cause other symptoms too, and the pattern of the tingling helps tell them apart. In pregnancy, retained fluid is one of the factors that can lead to carpal tunnel syndrome \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000433.htm) \].

## Frequently asked questions


### What vitamin am I lacking if my hands tingle?


The vitamin most often linked to tingling hands is vitamin B12. A low B12 level that lasts a long time can damage nerves and cause numbness and tingling in the hands and feet. Low levels of vitamins B1, B6 and folic acid can also cause tingling. Too much vitamin B6, usually from supplements, is another known cause, and a low copper level is a rarer one. A vitamin B12 blood test, often with methylmalonic acid (MMA), is the usual first check.


### When should I worry about tingling in my hands?


Call 911 for sudden numbness or weakness in the face, arm or leg, especially on one side, or for sudden confusion, trouble speaking, trouble seeing, trouble walking or a severe headache. These are stroke signs. Also call 911 if tingling comes with weakness, follows a head, neck or back injury, or comes with loss of bladder or bowel control. Contact a provider if the tingling has no obvious cause, keeps coming back, or comes with neck, forearm or finger pain.


### Why are both of my hands tingling?


Tingling in both hands at once points toward something that affects nerves throughout the body rather than pressure on one nerve. Common examples are a low vitamin B12 level, high blood sugar from diabetes, an underactive thyroid, kidney disease, a low calcium level and too much vitamin B6. Carpal tunnel syndrome can also affect both hands. Fast breathing during anxiety or a panic attack can cause brief tingling in both hands too.


### What causes tingling in the hands and feet?


Tingling in both the hands and the feet is the typical pattern of peripheral neuropathy, damage to the nerves that run to the arms and legs. Diabetes is the most common cause in the US, and its symptoms usually start in the toes and feet before reaching the hands. Low vitamin B12, too much vitamin B6, chronic kidney disease, an underactive thyroid, heavy alcohol use and some medicines are other causes. Blood tests can check most of them.


### Why do my hands go numb while I sleep?


Hands that go numb at night usually come from pressure on a nerve, for example from sleeping on a bent wrist or leaning on an elbow. Numbness in the thumb, index, middle and part of the ring finger fits carpal tunnel syndrome, and numbness in the little finger fits pressure on the ulnar nerve at the elbow. Ulnar nerve numbness can wake you from sleep, and a wrist splint at night is a common first step for carpal tunnel symptoms. Numbness that shakes out quickly is common. Numbness that happens most nights is worth having checked.
